full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: In this appeal by leave, at the instance of the defendant-tenant, the only question for consideration is, whether WASA charge payable by the tenant along with the 'rent' is part of the rent and non-deposit thereof under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1986 (Ordinance No. XXII of 1986) briefly, the Ordinance, would render the deposit of rent complete and invalid making the tenant liable for eviction. 

 2. Material facts necessary for disposal of this appeal, briefly are, that the appellant has been running its business as a monthly tenant since 1965 in Room No. 10 of the suit-building under successive owners thereof, the original owner being M/s. Issa Brothers. The last tenancy agreement was dated 2.2.1984 entered into between the appellant and the then owner Hassan Faruque and the said agreement was to expire on 31.12.1985. It was stipulated in the said agreement that the appellant would pay the monthly rent of Taka 1098 and in addition to that it would pay a fixed amount of Tk. 60 as WASA charge. It was also stipulated that after the expiry of the agreement the parties would be at liberty to renew the same. 

 3. It is admitted that the plaintiff-respondent after purchasing the suit-building served notice upon the appellant on 11.11.1985 informing it about the respondent's purchase of the suit building and further calling upon it to enter into a fresh agreement. The appellant paid rent to the respondent for the months of November and December 1985 at the rate of Taka 1098 per month. It however did not enter into any further agreement with the respondent whereupon the respondent by serving notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 21.1.1987 asked the appellant to vacate the room in question by the end of February 1987 and on its failure so to do instituted the suit being Civil Suit No. 722 of 1987 in the 4th Court of Assistant Judge. Dhaka for its eviction on the ground of default in payment of rent.. 

 4. The appellant contested the suit by filing a written statement alleging, inter alia, that no fresh agreement could be made with the respondent because of some unacceptable terms and conditions offered by him. The appellant offered rent for the month of January 1986 between the 2nd and 4th but the respondent refused to accept the same. The appellant sent the rent for the month of January 1986 on 6.1.1986 by postal money order which came back undelivered on 10.1.1986 whereupon the appellant deposited the rent for January 1986 within 15 days in the office of House Rent Controller. Dhaka in House Rent Case No. 80 of 1986. The appellant also sent the rent for the month of February by money order on 6.2.1986 and on its refusal has been regularly depositing the monthly rent in the aforesaid HR Case No. 80 of 1986. The appellant is accordingly, not a defaulter as alleged. 

 7. It appears from the impugned judgment that the learned Judge found that the respondent had received the rent for the months of November and December 1985 from the appellant subject to fresh lease agreement but it was not properly explained as to what factors had prevented the appellant to enter into a fresh agreement with the new landlord, namely, the plaintiff. It was argued on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent that the appellant was, in any case liable for eviction inasmuch as neither it paid the rent nor deposited the same even at the old rate in that it did not deposit Tk. 60 which it was liable to pay as WASA charge along with the rent and thus the same was not a valid deposit. 

 8. The main question which, therefore, came up for consideration before the learned Judge was whether Taka 60.00 as WASA charge payable along with the rent to the landlord as per agreement dated 2.2.1984 would be part of the rent for the purpose of deposit under section 19 of the Ordinance. After considering sections 9, 18(5) of the Ordinance and the case of Maherunnessa vs. A Latif 38 DLR (AD) 196 the learned Judge held thus: 

      "Although WASA charge is not rent within the meaning of 'rent' as defined in the Ordinance, yet WASA charge of Taka 60.00 as per terms of their tenancy will, in my opinion, form part of payment of the 'whole' rent otherwise the payment of whole rent will remain incomplete. So, the deposit of Taka 1098.00 as rent has to be made together with Taka 60.00 as WASA charge as per terms of tenancy. But it appears that the defendant-petitioner has not done so. Thus, the deposit of rent as made by the defendant-petitioner is not a complete nor a valid deposit." 

 11. We have perused the copy of the lease agreement dated 2.2.1984 which has been produced by Mr. Moksudur Rahman, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent. It is clearly provided in Clause (2) of the said agreement that the tenant will be a monthly, ordinary ejectable tenant under the owner in respect of the demised premises at a monthly rental of Taka 1098.00 only at the rate of Taka 3.00 only per sft. with effect from 1.1.1984 upto 31.12.1985 on the same terms and conditions as laid down in the previous agreement dated 7.1.1981. 

 12. Clause (5) provides that WASA charge will be paid at the rate of Taka 60.00 only per month by the tenants along with the rent. In case of enhancement by the Government the rate will be enhanced with the consent of the tenant. 

 13. Rent has not been defined in the Ordinance but in the latest Ordinance i.e. it has been only provided. Under section 19 of the Ordinance a tenant may deposit such rent as is referred to in section 18 when a landlord refuses to accept the same remitted by postal money order. Now section 18 for the present purpose may be extracted as follows: 18. No order for ejectment ordinarily to be made if rent paid at allowable rate: (1) Not withstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (IV of 1882). or the Contract Act, 1872 (IX of 1872), no order or decree, for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and performs the conditions of the tenancy: (1) (2) (3) (4)(5) No tenant shall be entitled to the benefit of this section in respect of any premises unless he pays the rent due by him in respect of such premises to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance within the time fixed in the contract with his landlord or, in the absence of such contract, by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable, or in the cases provided for in section 19, unless the tenant has deposited such rent or any subsequent rent in respect of such premises as provided in that section together with, in the case mentioned in sub-section (1) (b) of that section, the cost of transmission referred to in that sub-section within the time specified in that section. Explanation: (6) For the purposes of this section, the rent allowable by this Ordinance in relation to any premises means- 

 (a) Where the standard rent in respect of such premises has been fixed by the Controller under section 15, the standard rent so fixed; 

 (b) where such standard rent has not been fixed, the rent agreed upon between the landlord and the tenant to be paid in respect of such premises, or when the rent so agreed upon exceeds the standard rent of such premises, so much of the rent so agreed upon as does not exceed the standard rent. 

 14. In order to avoid eviction from any premises a tenant, inter alia, has to pay rent due from him in respect of such premises to the full extent allowable by the Ordinance and in certain circumstances he may also deposit the rent with the Controller under section 19. It is clear from such-section (6) above that for the purpose of section 18 the rent allowable by the Ordinance in relation to any premises, inter alia, means where standard rent has not been fixed, the rent agreed upon between the landlord and the tenant to be paid in respect of such premises. In the present case admittedly no standard rent has been fixed by the Controller and the rent agreed upon by the parties is fixed at Taka 1098.00 per month as per the lease agreement dated 2.2.1984. This amount then is the rent which the tenant is liable to pay to the landlord or make a deposit of the same under section 19. Charges and rates which a tenant is usually liable to pay for the utilities such as electricity, water, gas, etc, are not part of the rent of the premises. These payments are generally made to the authorities who provide for the said utilities. A landlord is not entitled to the said charges or rates for the simple reason that he does not supply the same to the tenant. 

 15. Mr. Moksudur Rahman, however, supported the view taken by the High Court Division contending that WASA charge in the present case which the appellant was liable to pay to the landlord at a fixed rate of Taka 60.00 per month under the agreement was part of the total rent and non-deposit thereof along with the monthly rent of Taka 1098.00 with the Controller had made the appellant a defaulter, the deposit made being not complete and valid. In this connection he has drawn our attention to section 9 of the Ordinance and the decision of this Division referred to above which was considered by the learned Judge of the High Court Division. Section 9 provides that where any municipal rate, tax, etc, is payable by the tenant and the landlord agrees, under the terms of the tenancy, to pay such rate, tax, etc, the amount so agreed to be paid by the landlord shall be payable by the tenant to the landlord in addition to the standard rent. Similarly, section 8 provides that where some addition, improvement, etc. has been made to any premises at the landlord's expense or any furniture has been supplied by the landlord for use in any premises, after the premises were let out, such additional amount as may be agreed upon between the landlord and the tenant in consideration of the additional improvement, etc., as the case may be, shall be payable by the tenant to the landlord in addition to the standard rent. Although the said amount/additional amount has not been clearly described as rent but reading the provisions of the said section which appear under Chapter III under the heading: Provisions Regarding Rent and Salami, and the 'Form' of rent receipt as provided under Rule 6 of the Premises Rent Control Rules, 1964, it is reasonable to hold that they may be said to form part of the rent as allowable by the Ordinance. Those amounts will be payable even if they are in excess of the standard rent. In our decision as referred to above it was not decided whether the additional payments were part of the rent but one of the questions decided was whether the agreement itself was void since it contained a clause that the municipal tax for the premises would be payable by the tenant. There are indications, however, in that decision which support the view that we are taking now that the amount/additional amount as referred to in sections 8 and 9 payable by the tenant would be part of the rent which the Ordinance allows. WASA charge being not included in either of the said sections, there appears to be no basis for holding that the same should be treated as part of the rent allowable under the Ordinance. 

 16. Mr. Moksudur Rahman submitted that as the term 'rent' has not been defined in the Ordinance it must be taken to have been used in its ordinary dictionary meaning and the term 'rent' is comprehensive enough to include all payments agreed by the tenant to be paid to the landlord for the use of any amenities agreed between the parties to be provided by and at the cost of the landlord. In support of his submission Mr. Rahman relied upon (1) Residence Limited vs. Surendra Mohan Banerjee 1951 Calcutta Law Journal (Vol. 87) 322 (2) SK Chatterjee vs. Residence Limited 58 CWN 607 and (3) Karnani Properties Limited vs. Miss Augustine AIR 1957 SC 309. 

 17. In the first case one of the contentions raised was that the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller to fix the 'standard rent' of the 'premises' would not include any payment for the services rendered by the landlord appellant. A furnished flat was let out at a lump sum rent of Rs.190.00 per month and by the terms of the tenancy agreement the landlord was bound to provide the tenant with electricity for various purposes, namely, lights, fans, cooking stoves, refrigerators, irons, etc., the services of a lift and free services of sweepers, plumbers, carpenters, darwans, etc. 

 18. The contention was not accepted and it was observed that the word 'rent' is not defined in the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act 1950 and therefore it must be given its ordinary grammatical meaning. When a flat is let, with the landlord agreeing to provides certain free services, what is let is the flat and what is paid is paid for the flat with the landlord providing certain amenities or performing certain obligations. What is paid is rent for the flat and no part of it can be truly regarded as payment for the services. It was held further that what is paid as rent under an agreement is paid for the premises together with the benefits of the landlord's covenants and that payment is at common law in England and under ordinary tenancy law in India the rent of the premises and must be regarded as the 'rent' of the premises as that term is used in the Rent Control Act. Rs.190.00 in that case was held to be the rent for the premises "and it is not the less rent proper because the landlord in the tenancy agreement had undertaken to do certain acts". 

 19. In the second case, the same landlord contended that charges for sweepers' services cannot be added to rent because standard rent has to be fixed in respect of 'premises' as defined by section 2(8) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950. The contention was rejected relying on the first case. The tenants agreed to pay the contractual rents including charges for furniture and services. It was held that the word "rent" has not been defined by the Act and in the absence of any definition it must be taken to mean any amount which is agreed to be paid by the tenant as consideration for occupation of the premises. 

 20. In the third case, the Supreme Court of India held in the same line as in the above two cases that the term "rent" is comprehensive enough to include all payments agreed by the tenant to be paid to his landlord for the use and occupation not only of the building and its appurtenances but also of furnishings, electric installations and other amenities agreed between the parties to be provided by and at the cost of the landlord. 

 21. On principle we take the same view that whatever amount is paid by the tenant to his landlord in terms of the contract as a consideration for the amenities, benefits and services to be provided by and at the cost of the landlord in connection with the use and occupation of the premises will form part of the "rent" within the meaning of sub-section (6) of section 18 of the Ordinance. The difference between the instant case and the cases relied upon, however, will be at once clear if we look at the agreements in any of those cases and that in the present case. For example, in the Supreme Court case, the relevant clause in the agreement reads: 

 That the tenant shall occupy the said flat paying therefore unto the Bank a monthly rent of Rs.100 including hire of 2 AC fans and extra Government duty on electric current without any reduction or abatement to be paid at the bank on or before the 7th of succeeding month for which the rent is due and that the said rent is inclusive of charges for current for fans, lights, radio and electric stove not exceeding 600 Watts for heating meals and making tea only, use of lift, hot and cold water, the owner and occupier's shares of Municipal Taxes." 

 22. In the present case, monthly rent has been fixed at Taka 1098.00 for the demised premises and by a separate clause it is provided that WASA charge will be paid at the rate of Taka 60.00 only per month along with the rent. Clearly the landlord did not undertake to provide water for the occupation of the premises for which the tenant had agreed to pay. The stipulation was that the tenant would pay the water bill but for the convenience of payment to WASA as there were other tenants in the premises and perhaps there, was no separate meter for each tenant, the tenant was required to pay WASA charge at a fixed rate of Taka 60.00 per month "along with the rent". That this is so will be clear from the plaintiffs own evidence. PW 1 deposing for the landlord said in chief that rent of the shop room was Taka 1098.00 per month and WASA charge Taka 60.00 In cross-examination he admitted that the defendant has paid rent for the months of November and December 1985 for which receipt had been given but there was no mention of WASA charge. Separate receipts were given for WASA and electric bills for the months of November and December 1985. Therefore it is clear that the tenants paid the water and electric bills for their respective shops but for facility and convenience of payment they were required to pay a lump sum per month to the landlord on that account along with the rent. That amount which is not due to the landlord on account of any amenity, benefit or service rendered by him cannot be said to be included in term "rent". The decisions relied upon by Mr. Moksudur Rahman, though good in principle, but do not help him in the facts of the present case. The landlord could complain of breach of the agreement if the WASA charge was not paid as agreed upon but non-payment or non-deposit of the 'WASA charge' along with the rent would not make him defaulter for non-payment of rent or for not making a valid deposit. 

 23. Therefore, we do not agree that WASA charge was a part of the rent and the deposit made as in the present case was not a complete or valid deposit.
